fetched_contents.text: Discursive psychology Form of discourse analysis For other uses, see Discursive (disambiguation). Discursive psychology (DP) is a form of discourse analysis that focuses on psychological themes in talk, text, and images. As a counter to mainstream psychology's treatment of discourse as a "mirror" for people's expressions of thoughts, intentions, motives, etc., DP's founders made the case for picturing it instead as a "construction yard" wherein all such presumptively prior and independent notions of thought and so on were built from linguistic materials, topicalised and, in various less direct ways, handled and managed.[1] Here, the study of the psychological implies commitment not to the inner life of the mind, but rather, to the written and spoken practices within which people invoked, implicitly or explicitly, notions precisely like "the inner life of the mind".[2] Discursive psychology therefore starts with psychological phenomena as things that are constructed, attended to, and understood in interaction. An evaluation, say, may be constructed using particular phrases and idioms, responded to by the recipient (as a compliment perhaps) and treated as the expression of a strong position. In discursive psychology, the focus is not on psychological matters somehow leaking out into interaction; rather, interaction is the primary site where psychological issues are live. It is philosophically opposed to more traditional cognitivist approaches to language. It uses studies of naturally occurring conversation to critique the way that topics have been conceptualised and treated in psychology. History The origins of what is now termed "discursive psychology" can arguably be traced to the late 1980s, and the collaborative research and analysis sessions that took place as part of Loughborough University's then newly formed Discourse and Rhetoric Group (DARG).[3] A key landmark was the publication of Jonathan Potter and Margaret Wetherell's classic text Discourse and social psychology: Beyond attitudes and behaviour in 1987. Charles Antaki, writing in the Times Higher Education Supplement, described the impact of this book: > Potter and Wetherell have genuinely presented us with a different way of working in social psychology. The book's clarity means that it has the power to influence a lot of people ill-at-ease with traditional social psychology but unimpressed with (or simply bewildered by) other alternatives on offer. It could rescue social psychology from the sterility of the laboratory and its traditional mentalism. The linguistic reorientation associated with discursive psychology drew on intellectual movements that challenged traditional psychological explanation, including post-structuralism, postmodernism, Foucault’s analyses of knowledge/power, theories of ideology, Lacanian psychoanalysis, microsociology, and social constructionism. It was further informed by analytic traditions such as conversation analysis, ethnomethodology, classical rhetoric, the sociology of science, Rom Harré’s ethogenics, and speech act theory.[4] The field itself was originally labeled as DP during the early 1990s by Derek Edwards and Potter at Loughborough University. It has since been developed and extended by a number of others, including (but by no means limited to): Charles Antaki, Malcolm Ashmore, Frederick Attenborough, Bethan Benwell, Steve Brown, Carly Butler, Derek Edwards, Alexa Hepburn, Eric Laurier, Hedwig te Molder, Sue Speer, Liz Stokoe, Cristian Tileaga, Sally Wiggins and Sue Wilkinson. Discursive psychology draws on the philosophy of mind of Gilbert Ryle and the later Ludwig Wittgenstein, the rhetorical approach of Michael Billig, the ethnomethodology of Harold Garfinkel, the conversation analysis of Harvey Sacks and the sociology of scientific knowledge of those like Mike Mulkay, Steve Woolgar and Bruno Latour. The term "discursive psychology" was designed partly to indicate that there was not just a methodological shift at work in this form of analysis, but also, and at the same time, that it involved some fairly radical theoretical rethinking. Study Discursive psychology conducts studies of both naturally occurring and experimentally engineered human interaction that offer new ways of understanding topics in social and cognitive psychology such as memory, identity and attitude. Although discursive psychology subscribes to a different view of human mentality than is advanced by mainstream psychology, Edwards and Potter's work was originally motivated by their dissatisfaction with how psychology had treated discourse. In many psychological studies, the things people (subjects) say are treated as windows (with varying degrees of opacity) into their minds. Talk is seen as (and, in experimental psychology and protocol analysis, used as) descriptions of people's mental content. In contrast, discursive psychology treats talk as social action; that is, we say what we do as a means of, and in the course of, doing things in a socially meaningful world. Thus, the questions that it makes sense to ask also change.[5] DP-in-action: an illustration DP can be illustrated with an example from Edwards' research on script formulations.[6] Traditional social psychology treats scripts as mentally encoded templates that guide action. Discursive psychology focuses on the foundational issue of how a description is built to present a course of action as following from a standardized routine. Take the following example from a couple counselling session (the transcription symbols here were developed by Gail Jefferson). The Counsellor says: "before you moved over here how was the marriage". After a delay of about half a second, Connie, the wife who is being jointly counselled, replies "Oh to me all along, right up to now, my marriage was rock solid. fetched_contents.text: Language and persuasion: A discursive psychological approach - Humă - 2023 - Social and Personality Psychology Compass 1 INTRODUCTION Across the social sciences, there is a wealth of research on the role that language plays in persuasion in interpersonal communication. The majority of these studies have been conducted in laboratories using experimental methods, have taken a social cognitive perspective, and have focused on identifying the effects that particular linguistic practices have on how persuasive messages are understood, processed, and ultimately complied with. This approach relies on an implicit view of language as furnishing the building blocks of messages within a “conduit” model of communication as information exchange (Maynard & Turowetz, 2013; Potter, 2021; Potter & te Molder, 2005). Epistemologically, individuals' language-in-use is treated as “a window on the mind” (Edwards & Potter, 1993, p. 23); that is, a means for accessing otherwise inaccessible thoughts and feelings. By contrast, less attention has been paid to how language is used to shape authentic and spontaneous social conduct in settings, like sales encounters, business meetings, or diplomatic/political negotiations, where persuasion occurs naturally. In these often high-stakes interactions, persuasion is built into the fabric of the conversation, intertwined with other co-occurring activities, and often obfuscated or disguised as, for example, advice giving. The roles of persuasion “source” and “target” are less-clear cut and can change throughout the conversation. To understand how persuasion is accomplished in real-life settings, we need to examine authentic data, collected from real-life interactions. Therefore, we need a framework that is equipped to illuminate the organisation of such conversations. In this paper, I will attempt to argue that, when studying persuasion in interpersonal interactions, a discursive psychological approach that pays attention to the sequential properties of conversations is better suited than a social cognitive approach for investigating and theorising the interactional structures underpinning persuasion and the role of language therein. Discursive psychology (DP) and other related approaches like conversation analysis (CA) treat language as the medium in and through which individuals perform social actions in interaction. This implicates a fundamental epistemological shift in the relationships between language and psychological phenomena, which so far has rendered cognitive and discursive psychology difficult to reconcile (Humă, Alexander, et al., 2020; Potter & te Molder, 2005). While considerable attention has already been paid to DP's treatment of language (inter alia Edwards, 1997; Edwards & Potter, 1993; Potter, 1996), two key aspects are worth unpacking here: namely how language is used to build social actions and how language provides a medium for the collaborative organisation of social interactions (Garfinkel, 1967). To that end, let us look at a short fragment from a real-life sales call between a prospective customer (“prospect” in sales parlance) and a salesperson. The conversation has been transcribed using the Jefferson (2004) transcribing conventions designed to capture the details of speech production such as silence, emphasis, and pitch, which have been found consequential for the organisation of social interactions (Hepburn & Bolden, 2017). At the beginning of the conversation, the salesperson (S in the transcript) had disavowed the commercial nature of the call, and now, almost a minute into the conversation, we get the following exchange. Extract 1. Tech 121 * 1 P: So you're trying to sell me something then. * 2 (0.4) * 3 S: ↑No=↑no:.=I just wanted to drop some details off so you * 4 can keep it on file. First, let us zoom in on the treatment of language as action. Take the prospect's utterance “So you're trying to sell me something then.”. Instead of speculating about whether this turn at talk might have been brought about by the speaker's sudden realisation that his interlocutor is indeed after a sale, an action-oriented approach to language asks what the prospect is doing at this very moment with this utterance. Key to answering this question are the minutiae details of the utterance, for example, the turn-initial “so”, which marks the rest of the turn as an inference derived from immediately prior talk (Schiffrin, 1987) and the turn-final “then” which implicitly sets up a contrast between the current characterisation of the salesperson's conduct and her prior disavowal of selling. Together with the emphasised person reference “you”, these features point towards the utterance working as an accusation leveraged by the prospect against the salesperson for what is constructed as duplicitous conduct. Further evidence is also available in the salesperson's turn, as I will show shortly. Let us now turn to how language provides a medium for interaction. Focusing on the salesperson's turn, we can note it is designed as a response to the prior utterance. This is not a trivial observation. Whatever the salesperson's agenda may be and whether she is working off a script or not, in this moment in the conversation she is accountable for responding to the prospect's accusation (Atkinson & Drew, 1979; Schegloff, 2007). Furthermore, whatever she does in this responsive slot, her turn will be interpreted as a reaction to the accusation. Discursive psychology treats stance expressions as central to how speakers shape interaction by positioning themselves and managing how others interpret their claims. In the evidence provided, stance is presented not as a fixed psychological state but as a social practice through which speakers construct and negotiate psychological phenomena such as belief, certainty, and evidence. The Wikipedia overview states that discursive psychology “starts with psychological phenomena as things that are constructed, attended to, and understood in interaction” and that it treats talk as social action rather than as a window into preexisting mental content [N1-F1]. This means stance expressions are analyzed as interactive resources used to define the world under description, including mental states and epistemic commitments, rather than as direct reflections of inner life [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes that discursive psychology critiques mainstream psychology’s treatment of discourse as a “mirror” for people’s thoughts and instead pictures it as a “construction yard” where psychological notions are built from linguistic materials [N1-F1]. This conceptualization directly supports the claim that stance is treated as a resource for positioning and shaping interaction.

On epistemic evaluation, certainty, and evidentiality, the evidence is explicit. The “Epistemic stance and evidentiality” excerpt describes the direct subjective expression of a speaker’s cognitive state and the objective evidential expression of how information is presented [N3-R5]. The same evidence also notes that evidential markers are linguistic devices that indicate information sources and that studies show they have an effect on how information is treated [N3-R4]. The Corpus Pragmatics excerpt on stance markers includes examples such as certainty adjectives that convey high degree of certainty/commitment, indicating that stance is tied to evaluative force and evidential confidence [N3-R3]. This means discursive psychology connects stance to epistemic orientation: speakers signal not only what they believe but also how confident they are and what kind of evidence supports their claims. The evidence therefore supports the claim that stance is connected to epistemic evaluation, certainty, and evidentiality [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Discursive psychology distinguishes stance from persuasion and attitude by focusing on how language is used to manage social action and interaction rather than on persuasion as a psychological process or attitude as a stable disposition. The “Language and persuasion” article notes that discursive psychology treats language as the medium in and through which individuals perform social actions in interaction, which implicates a fundamental epistemological shift [N1-F2]. It also contrasts discursive psychology with the social cognitive approach, which treats language as a conduit for information exchange and views language-in-use as “a window on the mind” [N1-F2]. This matters because stance is not reduced to persuasion’s persuasive effect or attitude’s cognitive content; instead, it is analyzed as part of the sequential organization of talk and the ways speakers position themselves in interaction. The same source argues that a discursive psychological approach is better suited than a social cognitive approach for investigating the interactional structures underpinning persuasion [N1-F2]. This distinction is also visible in the comparison with attitude and persuasion in the broader evidence: attitude change and persuasion are usually framed as cognitive or motivational events that mediate the impact of communication on attitudes and behavior, whereas discursive psychology focuses on the interactional organization of language itself [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. In short, discursive psychology treats stance as a resource for positioning and interactional management, whereas persuasion and attitude are framed as psychological outcomes or mechanisms of influence [N1-F2][N4-R2].

The evidence also supports the claim that stance mediates disagreement, agreement, and social alignment. The “Language and persuasion” article explicitly uses a sales call example in which the prospect’s accusation (“So you're trying to sell me something then”) functions as an action against the salesperson’s conduct, and the salesperson’s response is interpreted as a reaction to that accusation [N1-F2]. In this case, stance is not neutral; it is used to align or misalign with the other speaker’s characterization of the situation. Similarly, the “Annotating Speaker Stance in Discourse” study aims to identify speaker stance in discourse and provide an analytical resource for it, suggesting that stance is a key mechanism for expressing and evaluating claims in interaction [N3-R1]. The multimodal evidence also shows that epistemic stance is communicated verbally and nonverbally, including prosodic and gestural patterns, which means stance can shape alignment through both verbal and embodied cues [N3-R2]. This indicates that stance expressions are not just about what is said but also about how alignment is negotiated across interactional participants [N3-R2][N3-R1].

Stance is negotiated through turn management and interactional repair, as evidenced by the methodological emphasis on conversation analysis. The “Conversation analysis” source states that CA investigates the methods members use to achieve mutual understanding and focuses on the sequential organization of talk, turn-taking, repair mechanisms, and sequence organization [N2-R4][N2-R5]. The same source notes that CA studies naturally occurring conversations and focuses on the sequential organization of talk, turn-taking, repair mechanisms, and sequence organisation [N8-R3]. The “Origins and Orientations” text by Wooffitt notes the complex relationship between conversation analysis and discourse analysis, which is relevant because discursive psychology uses conversation analysis as a methodological tool to study naturally occurring interaction [N2-R1]. This means stance is not analyzed in isolation; it is embedded in the interactional structure of talk, including how turns are allocated, how speakers repair misunderstandings, and how sequences are organized [N2-R4][N2-R5][N8-R3]. The evidence therefore supports the claim that stance is negotiated through turn management and interactional repair [N2-R4][N2-R5][N8-R3].

Finally, stance reveals speaker positioning and epistemic orientation because it shows how speakers define the world under description and how they orient toward evidence and certainty. The Wikipedia overview states that in discursive psychology, talk is treated as social action, and psychological phenomena are understood in interaction rather than as preexisting mental contents [N1-F1]. This directly links stance to speaker positioning: the way a speaker frames a claim, expresses certainty, or signals evidence shapes how they are positioned relative to the interlocutor and the topic under discussion. The evidence on epistemic stance and evidentiality also shows that speakers communicate epistemic stance through both verbal and nonverbal means, including prosodic and gestural patterns, which indicates that epistemic orientation is not confined to linguistic form alone [N3-R2][N3-R5]. ### 1) How discursive psychology conceptualizes stance expressions

The foundational sources in the branch report show that discursive psychology is concerned with psychological themes in talk, text, and images, and that it treats language as a medium for performing social actions in interaction [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This means that stance expressions are analyzed as interactive resources: they are not just what speakers say, but how they use language to define the world under description, including mental states, perceptions, motivations, and epistemic commitments [N1-F1].

### 1) How discursive psychology conceptualizes stance expressions

Discursive psychology treats stance as a resource speakers use to position themselves and shape interaction. The foundational sources in the branch report show that discursive psychology is concerned with psychological themes in talk, text, and images, and that it treats language as a medium for performing social actions in interaction [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This is important because it shifts the focus from inner psychology to social practice: stance is not about what a speaker “really” believes, but about how they express, negotiate, and manage that belief in interaction [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Stance is also connected to epistemic evaluation, certainty, and evidentiality. The branch report notes that stance can signal subjective cognitive states and objective evidential expression, and that evidential markers indicate information sources [N3-R5][N3-R4]. The report also includes examples such as certainty adjectives that convey a high degree of certainty/commitment, showing that stance is indexed by evaluative force and confidence [N3-R3]. In discursive psychology, this means speakers do not merely state a position; they signal whether it is certain, uncertain, evidential, or based on specific information sources [N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In short, stance is epistemically significant: it is how speakers orient toward evidence and certainty.

Discursive psychology distinguishes stance from persuasion and attitude by focusing on how language is used to perform social action and organize interaction, rather than on persuasion as a psychological effect or attitude as a stable disposition. The branch report states that discursive psychology treats language as the medium in and through which individuals perform social actions in interaction, which implicates a fundamental epistemological shift [N1-F2]. It contrasts this with the social cognitive approach, which treats language as a conduit for information exchange and views language-in-use as “a window on the mind” [N1-F2]. The broader evidence on persuasion and attitude also shows that attitude and persuasion are usually framed as cognitive or motivational events that mediate the impact of communication on attitudes and behavior [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. In contrast, discursive psychology’s stance-theoretical sources emphasize that talk is the primary site where psychological issues are live and that language is the medium through which social actions are performed [N1-F1]. This means stance is treated as a social and interactional resource, whereas persuasion and attitude are framed as psychological outcomes or processes [N1-F2][N1-F1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 4) How discursive psychology compares stance analysis with other interpretive approaches

Discursive psychology compares stance analysis with other interpretive approaches by emphasizing that it is not merely a method for decoding meaning, but a way of treating language as social action and interactional organization. Overall, discursive psychology conceptualizes stance expressions as resources speakers use to position themselves and shape interaction, rather than as direct reflections of inner psychology. In short, discursive psychology is a stance-oriented approach to language use that treats stance as a social, interactional, and epistemic resource.
